text: Eduardo Le Monnier (born Edouard Stanislas Louis Le Monnier; 30 September 1873 in Paris – 14 February 1931 in Buenos Aires) was a French architect known for his work in Brazil, Uruguay, and primarily in Argentina.[1][2][3] He studied at the National School of Decorative Arts in Paris and moved to Brazil in 1894, where he worked on projects such as the General Carneiro station in Belo Horizonte and served as a professor at the School of Fine Arts in Curitiba. He arrived in Buenos Aires on 1 November 1896, where he developed most of his projects and concrete works. One of his first works there was the bakery La Burdalesa (Paraná nº 861/9, year 1898, already demolished). In 1901, he revalidated his diploma at the University of Buenos Aires and joined the Central Society of Architects (SCA). In 1902, he completed the Artistic Ironworks Motteau, featuring a remarkable Art Nouveau style (Avenida Juan de Garay no. 1272, demolished), followed by the headquarters of the mutual savings society La Bola de Nieve in Buenos Aires and in Rosario, province of Santa Fe (Cordoba and Laprida streets, year 1906). He won the Municipal Prize for the Best Facade in 1903 for the residence he built for Bartolomé Ginocchio on Lima Street No. 1642. Two years later, in 1905, he received the third prize for the façade of Felix Egusquiza's residence on Libertad Street No. 1394, and in 1907 he presided over the SCA. Due to these recognitions, several aristocratic families hired him to build large residences in the Barrio Norte; the most notable is the Fernández Anchorena Palace, now housing the Apostolic Nunciature, located at Avenida Alvear 1637, constructed between 1907 and 1909. Another residence, smaller but equally opulent, was built on Avenida de los Incas 3260 and still stands today. In the second half of the 1920s, up to the crisis of 1929, there was a significant rise in financial institutions in Argentina, which established large parent companies in downtown Buenos Aires, becoming the financial city that persists today. Le Monnier designed the headquarters of the Uruguayan Argentine Bank (Avenida Roque Sáenz Peña nº 501, year 1928) and the adjacent buildings of the Bencich brothers, owners of a construction company (Edificio Bencich, Av. Roque Sáenz Peña 615 and Edificio Miguel Bencich, Av. Roque Sáenz Peña nº 614/6). He also taught at the National Academy of Visual Arts and Architecture. He died in Buenos Aires on 14 February 1931, at the age of 58.[citation needed]
